To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The GABA cell phenotype is maintained by cell cycle regulation in the hippocampus, (2) the GABA cell network is dysregulated by changes in cell cycle and DNA damage repair in the hippocampus in SZ and BD, (3) the changes in cell cycle genes are specific to diagnosis and location within the tricortical pathway, and (4) the changes in DNA damage repair genes are specific to the diagnosis, location, and cell type.
cell cycle and DNA-repair gene expression are significantly altered in the SO of the CA3/2 region and in CA1 in SZ, and in the CA1 region of the SO in BD.
the regulation of cell cycle progression and DNA repair in hippocampal GAD67 neurons in bipolar disorder and schizophrenia is different from that in controls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the regulation of the hippocampal GAD67 gene, which is a marker of the GABA phenotype.
the identification of the genes that regulate the GABA cell function in the trisynaptically-projecting cells of hippocampus.

the molecular mechanisms that regulate the expression of genes that are critical for maintaining the GABA cell phenotypic state and DNA integrity in schizophrenia (SZ), bipolar disorder (BD), and normal control (NC) subjects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cell cycle regulation is differentially altered in both SZs and BD in a cell type specific manner.

the expression of genes that are associated with the cell cycle and DNA integrity are different in the SO of SZ and BDs, and that these differences are consistent with the hypothesis that SZ and BD are distinct disorders with different patterns of GABA cell dysfunction that involve fundamentally different gene networks.

cell cycle and DNA damage repair are significantly altered in SZ and BD, and that the regulation of the hippocampal GAD67 cell is differentially regulated in the trisynaptics pathway of both disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the regulation of cell cycle, and possibly DNA repair, in GABA cells is differentially regulated in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
GABA cells are regulated in different ways in SZ versus BD and that these changes are site-specific within the hippocampus.
the expression of cell cycle and G2/M checkpoint components are altered in SZ and BD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regulation of the cell cycle and DNA damage repair are altered in SZ and BD and that the changes in these processes are specific to diagnosis, location, and cell type.
the GABA cell dysfunction seen in SZs and BDS is likely to involve complex changes in cell cycle and DNA damage repair that are likely to involve different mechanisms in the two disorders.
there is a significant overlap in gene regulation between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, but the direction of change is opposite in these 2 disorders.
